Sunbae vs Hoobae: What These Korean Words Really Mean
You may have heard an idol say “sunbaenim.” Here is what it means, and how seniority felt to me at school, at work, and during military service in Korea.
Quick answer

If you watch K-pop interviews or variety shows, you have probably heard an idol call another artist {em1}sunbaenim{/em1} (선배님). Maybe you have wondered why they say it, especially when the person they are talking to is younger.

Here is the short answer: {strong1}sunbae{/strong1} (선배) means someone who started before you in the same school or field. {strong2}Hoobae{/strong2} (후배) means someone who came after you. Adding {em1}-nim{/em1} (님) makes{em2} sunbaenim{/em2} a respectful form of address.

That is the definition. What these relationships feel like in real life is another story. I grew up in Korea, went through school and military service, and worked at a Korean company. They each felt a little different.

What do sunbae and hoobae mean?

The National Institute of Korean Language’s {a1}dictionary entry for 선배{/a1} describes someone who started earlier in the same field, or entered the same school before you. Its {a2}entry for 후배{/a2} describes the person who came later.

You might also see these words written as {em1}seonbae{/em1} and {em2}hubae{/em2}. Those follow the official Korean romanization rules; {em3}sunbae{/em3} and{em4} hoobae{/em4} are spellings you will often see in English-language fan discussions.
One thing worth remembering: {strong1}being someone’s sunbae does not automatically make you their boss.{/strong1} They might simply have been in that field longer.
Can someone younger be your sunbae?
Yes. Imagine you join a university club at 22. Another member is 20, but they joined the club a year before you.
Even though they’re younger than you, they’re your sunbae in that club because they joined earlier and have been a member longer.
Being a sunbae in this situation is about how long you’ve been part of the club, not how old you are.

Age still matters in Korean social situations. It is just not the same thing as seniority. How people actually speak to each other may depend on their relationship, how well they know each other, and the setting. There is no one rule that answers every situation. If Korean age itself is confusing, our {a1}Korean age guide{/a1} helps with that part.
What it felt like at school
I grew up in a small town in Korea, where people tended to know each other, or at least know someone in common.
Manners were a big deal while I was growing up. Even with someone just one year ahead of me at school, I was careful to be polite. To be honest, I found seniors a little scary back then.

It was not because they had threatened me or done anything wrong. Just being around them could feel intimidating. Because the town was small and people seemed connected, I worried that getting on the wrong side of one senior could make things awkward with other seniors too.

Looking back, I do not know whether that would really have happened. But as a teenager, that was how it felt. Someone who grew up elsewhere or went to a different school might remember their seniors very differently.
At work, job titles add another layer
In a Korean office, people do not necessarily call each other sunbae and hoobae all day. Job titles are often more useful.

I used to work as a {em1}daeri{/em1} (대리), a job title often translated as assistant manager. Some employees in more junior positions were older than me, but they still called me {em2}daeri-nim{/em2} (대리님) out of respect for my position. I was polite to them too, because they were older.
For me, respect for someone’s position and respect for their age could exist side by side. A higher job title did not mean I could ignore someone’s age.

Your boss can be younger than you. Someone who joined first might hold a lower job title. The person training you, informally called a {em1}sasu{/em1} (사수) in some workplaces, might not be your manager either.
The military has its own seniority culture

Most Korean men are required to complete military service, with exceptions and different service arrangements. People do not all enlist at the same age, so a younger soldier can be someone else’s {em1}seonim{/em1} (선임), or senior soldier. The soldier who comes later is a {em2}huim{/em2} (후임), or junior soldier. In that relationship, age does not decide who is senior.

The way soldiers spoke to one another made that especially clear when I served. Senior soldiers commonly used {em1}banmal{/em1} (반말), or casual speech, with juniors. Juniors used much more formal speech when addressing seniors. We often called it the {em2}danakka{/em2} (다나까) style: expressions like “알겠습니다” or “알겠습니까?” rather than an everyday polite “-요” ending.

Military language has been changing, although that does not mean every unit speaks the same way today. A {a1}2018 article published by the National Institute of Korean Language{/a1} describes the pressure around strict military speech and discussions about using more everyday polite forms.

Military seniority also exists alongside official rank and the chain of command. Respecting a senior does not mean accepting bullying or unfair orders. Still, this is one of the clearest ways to see how age and seniority can differ in Korea.
Why K-pop idols say sunbaenim

In K-pop, the word often comes up when idols speak about artists who{a1} debuted{/a1} earlier or have worked in the industry longer. It is a way of acknowledging someone’s experience, not necessarily a sign that they know each other well.

Take BoA, who debuted in 2000. During her 20th-anniversary press event, she called veteran singer Na Hoon-a {em1}sunbaenim{/em1} while discussing what she had learned from watching his performance ({a1}Yonhap News{/a1}). In 2022, Yuna from the rookie group CSR called BoA {em2}sunbaenim{/em2} when naming her as a role model ({a2}CBS NoCut News{/a2}). BoA can be a senior to one artist and a junior to another.

At the 2025 debut showcase for {a1}CORTIS{/a1}, Martin spoke about having worked on music for senior artists at HYBE before finally standing on stage with his own group ({a2}Korea Economic Daily{/a2}).

That kind of respect feels familiar to me. Artists do not need to work at the same company to recognize someone who started in the same industry earlier. But their personal relationship is another question, and we cannot tell how close they are from the word {em1}sunbaenim{/em1} alone.
The good side and the difficult side

Seniority can be uncomfortable. I remember being nervous around seniors as a student, and I understand why the pressure to show respect can feel heavy at times. Just because a relationship has a senior and a junior does not mean those people will automatically get along.

But when people get closer, it can become a really good relationship. A senior may look after a junior, help them settle in, or share things they learned the hard way. The junior might come to trust them, and the two can become much less formal with each other. That side of the culture matters to me too.
A local take from HAEMIL
A local take from HAEMIL

When I hear someone say {em1}sunbaenim{/em1} now, I barely think about it. It is a word I have heard all my life. But I can see why it might be confusing if you did not grow up here. Being someone’s sunbae tells you something about when they started. It does not tell you everything about their relationship. That depends on the people themselves.
